author: high2
claim: Subgoal solved: the terminal-rank map i -> (I_i,D_i) is injective.
evidence: For arbitrary i<j, distinctness gives exactly one of x_i<x_j or x_i>x_j. In the first case, adjoining x_j after a longest increasing subsequence ending at x_i yields I_j>=I_i+1. In the second case, adjoining x_j after a longest decreasing subsequence ending at x_i yields D_j>=D_i+1. Thus at least one coordinate differs for every two positions.

links.subgoal: Prove injectivity of the terminal-rank map.
links.attempt_summary: Appending the later term strictly raises one coordinate.

glossary.I_i: Maximum length of a strictly increasing subsequence ending at x_i.
glossary.D_i: Maximum length of a strictly decreasing subsequence ending at x_i.

author: high2
claim: Subgoal solved: if every increasing and decreasing subsequence has length at most n, injectivity of the terminal-rank map contradicts the existence of n^2+1 positions.
evidence: Under the assumed length bounds, each I_i and D_i is an integer from 1 through n. Hence every pair (I_i,D_i) lies in {1,...,n} x {1,...,n}, which has n*n=n^2 members. Injectivity would place n^2+1 distinct position indices into this n^2-element set, contradicting the pigeonhole principle.

links.subgoal: Convert the absence of long monotone subsequences into a finite counting contradiction.
links.attempt_summary: Both ranks lie in an n by n grid but there are n^2+1 distinct rank pairs.

glossary.n: The positive integer in the target theorem.
glossary.I_i: Maximum length of a strictly increasing subsequence ending at position i.
glossary.D_i: Maximum length of a strictly decreasing subsequence ending at position i.

author: high
claim: Let (n) be a positive integer. Prove that every sequence of (n^2+1) distinct real numbers contains either a strictly increasing subsequence of length (n+1) or a strictly decreasing subsequence of length (n+1).
evidence:
Write the given sequence in its original order as x_1,x_2,...,x_{n^2+1}. For every index i in {1,2,...,n^2+1}, define p_i to be the greatest possible length of a strictly increasing subsequence whose last term is x_i, and define q_i to be the greatest possible length of a strictly decreasing subsequence whose last term is x_i. These greatest lengths exist because the sequence is finite and the one-term subsequence consisting of x_i is both strictly increasing and strictly decreasing.

Assume for contradiction that the sequence has neither a strictly increasing subsequence of length n+1 nor a strictly decreasing subsequence of length n+1. Then 1<=p_i<=n and 1<=q_i<=n for every i, so every ordered pair (p_i,q_i) belongs to {1,2,...,n} x {1,2,...,n}.

We prove that these ordered pairs are pairwise distinct. Let i and j satisfy 1<=i<j<=n^2+1. Because all terms of the original sequence are distinct, either x_i<x_j or x_i>x_j.

If x_i<x_j, choose a strictly increasing subsequence of length p_i ending at x_i; such a subsequence exists by the definition of p_i. Appending x_j to it is valid because j>i, and the appended value is larger than x_i. The resulting subsequence is strictly increasing, ends at x_j, and has length p_i+1. Therefore p_j>=p_i+1, so p_j is not equal to p_i.

If x_i>x_j, choose a strictly decreasing subsequence of length q_i ending at x_i. Appending x_j is valid because j>i, and the appended value is smaller than x_i. The resulting subsequence is strictly decreasing, ends at x_j, and has length q_i+1. Therefore q_j>=q_i+1, so q_j is not equal to q_i.

Thus (p_i,q_i) is not equal to (p_j,q_j) whenever i<j. Hence the n^2+1 indices give n^2+1 distinct ordered pairs in {1,2,...,n} x {1,2,...,n}. But that Cartesian product has exactly n*n=n^2 elements, which is impossible. This contradiction proves that at least one of the two required subsequences exists.

glossary.x_i: the term in position i of the given finite sequence
glossary.p_i: the maximum length of a strictly increasing subsequence ending at x_i
glossary.q_i: the maximum length of a strictly decreasing subsequence ending at x_i
glossary.i: an index of a term of the sequence

author: high2
claim: Complete proof of the target theorem by injectivity of terminal increasing/decreasing rank pairs.
evidence:
Let the sequence be x_1,x_2,...,x_{n^2+1}, listed in its given order.

For every index i with 1<=i<=n^2+1, define I_i to be the largest possible length of a strictly increasing subsequence whose final term is x_i, and define D_i to be the largest possible length of a strictly decreasing subsequence whose final term is x_i. These maxima exist because the one-term subsequence (x_i) is both strictly increasing and strictly decreasing, while every subsequence ending at x_i has length at most i.

Assume for contradiction that the sequence contains neither a strictly increasing subsequence of length n+1 nor a strictly decreasing subsequence of length n+1. Then every increasing subsequence and every decreasing subsequence has length at most n. Consequently, for every i,
1<=I_i<=n and 1<=D_i<=n.

We next prove that the n^2+1 ordered pairs (I_i,D_i) are all distinct. Choose indices i<j. Because all terms of the sequence are distinct, x_i and x_j are unequal. If x_i<x_j, choose a strictly increasing subsequence of length I_i ending at x_i. Appending x_j to it is legitimate because j is later than i and x_j>x_i. The result is a strictly increasing subsequence of length I_i+1 ending at x_j. Therefore I_j>=I_i+1, so I_j is not equal to I_i. If instead x_i>x_j, choose a strictly decreasing subsequence of length D_i ending at x_i. Appending x_j gives a strictly decreasing subsequence of length D_i+1 ending at x_j. Therefore D_j>=D_i+1, so D_j is not equal to D_i. In either case (I_i,D_i) is not equal to (I_j,D_j). Since every pair of distinct indices can be ordered as i<j, all n^2+1 ordered pairs are distinct.

However, the inequalities 1<=I_i<=n and 1<=D_i<=n show that each (I_i,D_i) belongs to the set {1,2,...,n} x {1,2,...,n}. This set has n*n=n^2 elements, so it cannot contain n^2+1 distinct ordered pairs. This contradiction shows that the assumption was false. Hence the original sequence contains a strictly increasing subsequence of length n+1 or a strictly decreasing subsequence of length n+1.

links.attempt_summary: Assuming both monotone lengths are at most n puts n^2+1 distinct rank pairs in an n^2-element grid.

glossary.n: The positive integer in the theorem.
glossary.x_i: The i-th term of the given sequence.
glossary.I_i: The maximum length of a strictly increasing subsequence ending at x_i.
glossary.D_i: The maximum length of a strictly decreasing subsequence ending at x_i.
glossary.i: A position index in the sequence.
glossary.j: A position index later than i.
